title: Recon & Digital Footprint
tagline: Know what the world can already see about you.
summary: Passive and semi-passive reconnaissance (OSINT) applied to your own footprint: GitHub history, domains you own, and metadata you've published. No exploitation yet — this rank is about seeing yourself the way an attacker would.

missions.title: GitHub Shadow
missions.objective: Enumerate everything a stranger could learn about you from your own public GitHub account, including secrets that were committed and later 'deleted' but still live in git history.

target.label: Your public GitHub account and repos

steps: List every public repo: `gh repo list <your-username> --limit 200`.
Clone each one locally, then run `gitleaks detect --source . -v` (or `trufflehog git file://.`) to catch secrets committed anywhere in history, even in commits you force-pushed over.
Check who you leaked to the commit log: `git log --all --format='%an <%ae>'` — personal email, machine hostname in commit signatures, etc.
Grep README/config files for internal hints: server names, staging URLs, TODO comments mentioning credentials or internal architecture.
Check `package.json`/lockfiles for any dependency pinned to a version with a known CVE (quick pass, doesn't need to be exhaustive).
Write a one-page recon report: what you found, how bad each finding is, and what you'd rotate/fix first.
legalBoundaries: Everything here is your own public data — pure read-only recon, nothing to authorize beyond owning the account.
If you find a real secret (API key, token), treat it as live: rotate it immediately, don't just note it and move on.

risks.label: You might find a genuinely valid, still-active credential
risks.mitigation: Rotate/revoke it the moment you confirm it works — don't leave it live to 'test more later'.

completionCriteria: A written recon report listing every exposure found (or explicitly 'none found') with a severity per item.
Any live secret discovered has been rotated.
writeupPrompts: What's the single most damaging thing a stranger could learn about you from your GitHub alone?
Which of these leaks would `gitleaks`/GitHub secret scanning have already caught automatically if enabled?

missions.title: Domain Ghost
missions.objective: Passive DNS/WHOIS/certificate-transparency recon against a domain you personally own or control, to see your real external attack surface.

target.label: A domain/subdomain you own (or a GitHub Pages / Vercel URL you control)

missions.resourceNote: Needs a domain you actually registered/control. If you don't have one yet, do a dry run against a GitHub Pages / Vercel preview URL you own instead — the DNS parts stay locked until you own a domain.
steps: `whois yourdomain.com` — check registrar, expiry date, exposed registrant contact (privacy-guard on?).
`dig yourdomain.com ANY` / separate A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS queries — map every record.
Check SPF/DMARC: `dig TXT yourdomain.com` and `dig TXT _dmarc.yourdomain.com` — missing/weak SPF+DMARC means anyone can spoof email 'from' your domain.
Subdomain enumeration via certificate transparency: browse crt.sh/?q=%.yourdomain.com — look for forgotten staging/dev subdomains still resolving.
If you have a public IP behind the domain, look it up on Shodan's free search to see what banners/ports are visible externally.
Write a hardening checklist from what you found (SPF/DMARC/DNSSEC, remove dead subdomains, enable registrar privacy).
legalBoundaries: Only domains you registered/administer — WHOIS/DNS/crt.sh lookups on domains you don't own are legal (public data) but out of scope for this mission's spirit; stay on your own assets.
Passive only: no active scanning of IPs/services you don't also own in this mission — save that for the Gold rank.

risks.label: None — fully passive, read-only public-record lookups

completionCriteria: A DNS/exposure report for the domain.
SPF/DMARC/DNSSEC hardening checklist, ideally actually applied at your registrar.
writeupPrompts: Did you find a forgotten subdomain still pointing at something? What would happen if you hadn't found it first?

missions.title: Metadata Leak Hunt
missions.objective: Find hidden metadata (GPS, author names, internal file paths, software versions) baked into files you've published publicly.

target.label: PDFs, images, or documents you've shared publicly

steps: Gather 5-10 files you've actually published (project screenshots, PDFs, portfolio images).
Run `exiftool -r ./your-files/` and read every field, not just the obvious ones.
Flag anything sensitive: GPS coordinates on photos, your real name/username in PDF 'Author' metadata, internal file paths (`C:\Users\realname\...`), software/version fingerprints.
Strip metadata from anything still live (`exiftool -all= file.jpg`) and re-publish if it's your call to do so.
legalBoundaries: Only your own published files.

risks.label: None — read-only local file inspection

completionCriteria: A list of files with sensitive metadata found.
A personal habit/checklist: strip metadata before publishing, from now on.
writeupPrompts: Which file surprised you the most?

missions.title: Secret Scraper — Écrire son propre détecteur de secrets dans l'historique Git
missions.objective: Au lieu d'utiliser seulement gitleaks, écrire un script (Node.js ou Python) qui analyse le log Git (`git log -p`) et recherche des patterns de secrets (clés AWS, tokens, mots de passe, etc.) en utilisant des regex et des règles simples. Comprendre ce que gitleaks fait sous le capot.

target.label: Your public GitHub account and repos

steps: Clone tes repos publics localement (déjà fait si tu as fait bronze-github-shadow avant).
Écris un script (Node.js ou Python) qui lit `git log -p` et recherche des patterns de secrets : AWS keys (AKIA...), tokens, mots de passe, clés API, etc. en utilisant des regex.
Comprends comment gitleaks détecte les secrets — compare ton approche avec gitleaks.
Ajoute des règles personnalisées pour les patterns spécifiques à tes projets.
Génère un rapport structuré : quels secrets trouvés, où, quelle gravité.
legalBoundaries: Only scan your own repositories.

risks.label: None — read-only local file inspection

completionCriteria: A working script that detects secrets in git history.
Comparison report: your approach vs gitleaks.
writeupPrompts: What patterns did you miss compared to gitleaks?
How would you extend your script to detect new types of secrets?

missions.title: Metadata Parser — Parser exiftool pour générer un rapport structuré
missions.objective: Dans le cadre de bronze-metadata-leak, écrire un script qui parse la sortie `exiftool -j` (JSON) et génère un rapport structuré des métadonnées sensibles présentes dans les fichiers publiés.

target.label: PDFs, images, or documents you've shared publicly

steps: Exécute `exiftool -j` sur tes fichiers publiés pour obtenir la sortie JSON.
Écris un script (Python ou Node.js) qui parse cette sortie JSON et identifie les champs sensibles : GPS, auteur, chemins de fichiers locaux, versions de logiciels.
Génère un rapport HTML ou Markdown avec les métadonnées trouvées et leur niveau de risque.
Compare ton rapport avec une lecture manuelle de exiftool — les deux donnent-ils les mêmes résultats ?
legalBoundaries: Only your own published files.

risks.label: None — read-only local file inspection

completionCriteria: A working script that parses exiftool JSON output and generates a structured report.
A comparison between manual and automated analysis.
writeupPrompts: What metadata surprised you the most in your own files?

title: Web Exploitation
tagline: Break the app before someone else does.
summary: OWASP Top 10 practice: first against target-range, a small deliberately-vulnerable app bundled in this repo so this rank never blocks on missing resources, then — carefully — against a real dev/staging copy of one of your own projects.

missions.title: The Vault
missions.objective: Bypass authentication and exfiltrate data from target-range's login form using SQL injection, then patch the query yourself.

target.label: target-range (bundled, local-only)

steps: Start the range locally: `bun run target-range` (never expose this port beyond localhost).
Open the login form, intercept the POST request in Burp/ZAP or just try it in the form directly.
Try a classic auth-bypass payload in the username field: `' OR '1'='1' -- `.
Confirm you're logged in as the first user in the table without knowing any password.
Point `sqlmap` at the vulnerable parameter (`sqlmap -u "http://localhost:4243/login" --data="username=x&password=y" --batch`) to enumerate the schema and dump the users table.
Open `target-range/src/routes/login.ts`, find the string-concatenated query, and rewrite it using a parameterized query. Re-run your bypass — confirm it now fails.
legalBoundaries: target-range is local-only and ships with a loud warning banner — never deploy it publicly, never point sqlmap at anything except your own localhost instance.

risks.label: target-range's own SQLite file gets corrupted/dumped
risks.mitigation: It's a throwaway seed DB — delete and reseed with `bun run target-range:seed` any time.

completionCriteria: A working auth-bypass PoC (screenshot or terminal capture).
A patched `login.ts` using parameterized queries, verified to block the same payload.
writeupPrompts: Why does a parameterized query fix this and string-escaping alone wouldn't be enough?

missions.title: Reflected Ghosts
missions.objective: Find and exploit reflected and stored XSS in target-range's comment/search feature.

target.label: target-range (bundled, local-only)

steps: On the search page, try `<script>alert(document.cookie)</script>` in the query string and see it reflected unescaped.
On the comments feature, post a stored payload like `` and reload as a different session to confirm it fires for other viewers.
Demonstrate impact against your own browser only: read `document.cookie` or `localStorage` from the injected script (never exfiltrate to a real external endpoint — log it to the console instead).
Fix it: add output encoding on render and a restrictive Content-Security-Policy header in `target-range/src/middleware.ts`. Re-test — confirm the payload now renders as inert text.
legalBoundaries: Local-only target. No real users or real cookies are ever at risk here.

risks.label: None beyond the local app itself

completionCriteria: Working reflected and stored PoCs.
A CSP header + output-encoding fix that blocks both.
writeupPrompts: What's the difference in blast radius between the reflected and the stored version of this bug?

missions.title: Broken Gate
missions.objective: Forge an admin JWT against target-range's intentionally weak token signing and reach an admin-only route.

target.label: target-range (bundled, local-only)

steps: Log in as a normal user, grab the JWT from the response/cookie.
Decode it (base64) and inspect the header/payload — note the `alg` and the `role` claim.
Try re-encoding the token with `alg: none` and no signature, or brute-force the (deliberately weak) HMAC secret with `hashcat -m 16500 <token> wordlist.txt`.
Set `role: admin` in the forged payload, hit `/api/admin/users` with it, and confirm access.
Fix `target-range/src/lib/jwt.ts`: use a long random secret from an env var, and explicitly allowlist the signing algorithm server-side instead of trusting the token's own `alg` header.
legalBoundaries: Local-only target.

risks.label: None beyond the local app itself

completionCriteria: A forged admin token that works, then a fix that makes it stop working.
writeupPrompts: Why is trusting the `alg` field inside the token itself a design flaw?

missions.title: Your Own Backyard
missions.objective: Run the same OWASP Top 10 checklist you just practiced against a real project of yours, on a local/dev copy only.

target.label: One of your real projects (local dev copy, not production)

missions.resourceNote: Depends on having a real project with a login form, API, or user input to test. If none of your current repos qualify yet, this stays optional/locked until you designate one — you mentioned you'll set that up.
steps: Spin up a local/dev copy of the project — never test a live production deployment with real user data.

Walk the OWASP Top 10 checklist against it: injection, broken auth, sensitive data exposure, XXE, broken access control, security misconfig, XSS, insecure deserialization, vulnerable dependencies, insufficient logging.
For every finding, capture a PoC and rate its severity.
Fix at least the highest-severity finding and re-test.
legalBoundaries: Local/dev copy only — a project you own end-to-end counts as self-authorized. If it ever has real users or real data, that data is off-limits: use seed/fake data.
Never point automated scanners (sqlmap, ZAP active scan) at a URL you don't control the hosting of.

risks.label: Accidentally running a destructive test against a production database
risks.mitigation: Point every tool at a local `.env` with a throwaway DB before you start; double-check the target URL/port every single time.

completionCriteria: A short pentest-style report: finding, severity, PoC, fix — for your own real project.
writeupPrompts: What did practicing on target-range first change about how you approached your own code?

missions.title: Coder son propre app vulnérable — Ajouter une nouvelle vulnérabilité à target-range
missions.objective: Prendre target-range (le serveur Bun local vulnérable) et y ajouter une nouvelle route vulnérable que tu codes toi-même. Par exemple : une SSRF (le serveur fait une requête vers une URL fournie par l'utilisateur sans validation), ou une injection NoSQL, ou une désérialisation dangereuse. Puis exploite cette vulnérabilité que tu as codée (comprendre les deux côtés : écrire le bug, l'exploiter, la patcher).

target.label: target-range (bundled, local-only) — extended by you

steps: Lis le code de target-range pour comprendre la structure existante (routes, middleware, db).
Ajoute une nouvelle route vulnérable au serveur (par exemple POST /fetch avec une SSRF : le serveur récupère une URL donnée et retourne le contenu sans validation).
Teste la nouvelle vulnérabilité : exploite-la manuellement avec curl.
Analyse : pourquoi cette vulnérabilité fonctionne-t-elle ? Quel est le mécanisme sous-jacent ?
Patch la vulnérabilité (validation de l'URL, allowlisting, etc.) et confirme que l'exploit ne fonctionne plus.
Note : ces étapes t'apprennent à coder une vulnérabilité, à l'exploiter, et à la corriger — les trois côtés de la sécurité offensive et défensive.
legalBoundaries: Local-only target. Only add vulnerabilities to target-range, never to a real service.

risks.label: None — local app, throwaway code

completionCriteria: A new vulnerable route added to target-range and documented.
Working exploit for that vulnerability.
Patched version that blocks the exploit.
writeupPrompts: What did you learn about the vulnerability by coding it yourself?
How does this vulnerability compare to the existing ones in target-range?

missions.title: Automatiser l'exploitation — Écrire ton propre script d'attaque contre target-range
missions.objective: Écrire un script (Node.js ou Python) qui, sans utiliser sqlmap, lance la requête SQLi avec différents payloads, parse la réponse, et détecte si l'injection a réussi (basé sur le contenu de la réponse, le code HTTP, etc.). Ce script devient ton propre 'mini sqlmap'.

target.label: target-range (bundled, local-only)

steps: Écris un script qui envoie des requêtes POST à /login avec différents payloads SQLi (dans le champ username).
Parse la réponse HTTP pour déterminer si l'injection a réussi (code 200 + contenu spécifique vs code 401).
Ajoute une fonctionnalité d'énumération : le script devine le nombre de colonnes, le nom de la table, etc. (comme le ferait sqlmap, mais manuellement).
Compare ton script avec sqlmap : lequel est plus rapide ? Lequel est plus précis ?
Optionnel : ajoute une fonction de détection de XSS dans le même script (réutilise le payload de silver-reflected-ghosts).
legalBoundaries: Local-only target. No automated tools against real services.

risks.label: None — local app only

completionCriteria: A working exploit script that automates SQLi detection.
Comparison report: your script vs sqlmap.
writeupPrompts: What did you learn about automated exploitation by writing your own script?
Would you use your script in a real engagement? Why or why not?

title: Network & Infrastructure
tagline: Map the wires before you pull them.
summary: Scanning and auditing your own LAN, Wi-Fi, and the traffic your own devices put on it. Everything here stays inside your own network boundary.

missions.title: Port Sweep
missions.objective: Map every device and open service on your own LAN, and flag anything unnecessarily exposed.

target.label: Your own home LAN / your own PC

steps: Find your LAN range (`ip a`, look at your subnet, e.g. 192.168.1.0/24).
`nmap -sV -sC 192.168.1.0/24` — service + version detection across the whole subnet.
For your own machine specifically: `ss -tulpn` (Linux/WSL) to see every listening process and port.
For each open service you don't recognize or need, decide: close it, firewall it, or document why it's intentional.
Write a network map + a 'ports closed' hardening list.
legalBoundaries: Your own LAN only. Scanning a network you don't own or administer — a coffee shop's Wi-Fi, a friend's router, a work network without written authorization — is illegal in most jurisdictions even if you never exploit anything found. Don't do it, ever, outside an authorized engagement.

risks.label: Aggressive scan flags/timing can trip IDS or destabilize flaky IoT devices
risks.mitigation: Use default timing (`-T3`) on a home network, avoid `-T5`/aggressive scripts against anything IoT.

completionCriteria: A network map of your LAN.
A hardening list of ports/services closed or firewalled.
writeupPrompts: What was open that you genuinely didn't expect?

missions.title: Wi-Fi Under the Microscope
missions.objective: Audit your own home Wi-Fi's security configuration end to end.

target.label: Your own home router / access point

missions.resourceNote: The passive checks (router admin panel review) always work. The active handshake-capture exercise needs a Wi-Fi adapter that supports monitor mode — flag this as a gear purchase if you want the full version.
steps: Log into your router's admin panel. Confirm encryption is WPA2/WPA3 (never WEP or open).
Check whether WPS is enabled — if so, disable it (WPS PINs are brute-forceable).
Confirm the router admin password isn't still the factory default.

If you have a monitor-mode-capable adapter: capture a WPA handshake from your own AP (`airodump-ng`) and test your own passphrase's strength offline with `aircrack-ng` against a wordlist — never against a network that isn't yours.
Write a hardening checklist: WPA3 if supported, WPS off, strong unique admin password, guest network isolated from IoT/main LAN.
legalBoundaries: Your own access point only. Capturing handshakes or attempting to crack Wi-Fi passwords for a network you don't own/administer is illegal.

risks.label: Deauth frames used during handshake capture will briefly drop your own devices off Wi-Fi
risks.mitigation: Do it during a maintenance window, not mid-videocall.

completionCriteria: A Wi-Fi hardening checklist, applied to your actual router.
writeupPrompts: How long would your current Wi-Fi passphrase realistically take to crack offline, and would a longer passphrase meaningfully change that?

missions.title: Man in Your Own Middle
missions.objective: Intercept traffic from a device you own on your own LAN to see what your own apps leak in cleartext.

target.label: A device you own (e.g. your own phone) on your own LAN

steps: On your PC, run `bettercap` on your LAN interface and ARP-spoof only your own second device (phone/tablet you own).
Capture the traffic with Wireshark while you use a few apps normally on that device.
Filter for HTTP (not HTTPS) traffic and look for any credentials, tokens, or personal data sent in cleartext.
Stop the spoof cleanly (`bettercap` restores ARP tables on exit) and confirm your device's connectivity is back to normal.
Write up any cleartext leaks found and recommend TLS/cert pinning fixes for anything you control the code of.
legalBoundaries: Only intercept a device you personally own and have full authority over. Never a roommate's, family member's, or coworker's device on the same network without their explicit, informed consent — even 'just to test' is not authorization.

risks.label: ARP spoofing can disrupt your own network traffic or, if the spoof isn't cleaned up, leave routing broken
risks.mitigation: Run it during a maintenance window; always let bettercap restore ARP tables before stopping; keep a router reboot as a fallback.

completionCriteria: A traffic report noting any cleartext credentials/tokens found (or confirming everything was encrypted).
writeupPrompts: Did any app you trusted turn out to be sending anything in cleartext?

missions.title: Coder son propre scanner de ports — Comprendre le TCP à bas niveau
missions.objective: Au lieu d'utiliser seulement nmap, écrire un scanner de ports TCP basique en Python (ou autre langage) qui utilise `socket.connect()` pour tester une plage de ports sur une cible. Comprendre ce qu'il se passe au niveau réseau (SYN, ACK, échec de connexion). Comparer avec nmap : rapidité, précision, discrétion.

target.label: Your own LAN (VM or home LAN)

missions.offlineNote: Faisable sur un réseau local (VM communicantes ou home LAN). Pas besoin d'internet.
steps: Écris un scanner de ports simple qui teste chaque port d'une plage (ex: 1-1024) sur une cible et indique si le port est ouvert (connexion acceptée) ou fermé (connexion refusée).
Teste ton scanner sur une cible locale (une VM, ou ton propre PC).
Compare les résultats avec nmap : quels ports manquent dans ton scanner ? Pourquoi ?
Améliore ton scanner : ajouter un délai entre les scans, une détection de service basique (envoyer un probe et lire la réponse).
Note: cet exercice t'apprend le protocole TCP et la programmation réseau.
legalBoundaries: Only scan your own network or devices you own.

risks.label: Scanning may trigger IDS on some networks

completionCriteria: A working port scanner in Python.
Comparison report: your scanner vs nmap.
writeupPrompts: What did you learn about TCP by writing your own scanner?
When would you use your scanner vs nmap in a real engagement?

title: System & Host Exploitation
tagline: Own the box — safely, in a box.
summary: Privilege escalation and password auditing, always inside disposable VMs with a clean snapshot — never on your daily-driver OS.

missions.title: Snapshot First
missions.objective: Build a disposable Linux VM lab you can break without any risk to your real machine.

target.label: A local VM (VirtualBox/VMware/UTM) or container

missions.resourceNote: Needs a hypervisor installed (VirtualBox, VMware, or Docker as a lighter alternative). Flagged as a prerequisite setup step for the rest of this rank.
steps: Install a hypervisor and create a minimal Linux VM with no network bridging beyond NAT (isolated from your LAN).
Take a clean snapshot the moment install finishes, before touching anything.
Rehearse the restore-from-snapshot flow once now, so it's muscle memory before you actually need it.
legalBoundaries: Everything from here on happens strictly inside this VM.

risks.label: None yet — this is just lab setup

completionCriteria: A running VM with a verified, restorable clean snapshot.

missions.title: PrivEsc Playground
missions.objective: Deliberately misconfigure your own VM, then escalate from a low-privilege user to root using standard enumeration techniques.

target.label: The VM from Snapshot First

missions.resourceNote: Depends on Snapshot First being done first.
steps: Create a non-root user, then deliberately introduce one misconfiguration: a SUID binary that shouldn't be SUID, a `sudo NOPASSWD` entry for a dangerous binary, or a cron job writable by your low-priv user.
Log in as the low-priv user and run `linpeas.sh` to enumerate the box the way an attacker would.
Use the flagged misconfiguration (cross-reference GTFOBins for the specific binary) to escalate to root.
Write up the exact escalation path, then fix the misconfiguration and confirm the same path no longer works.
Restore the snapshot when done so the VM is clean for the next mission.
legalBoundaries: Your own disposable VM only.

risks.label: None — isolated, disposable VM
risks.mitigation: Snapshot restore is your safety net.

completionCriteria: A root shell obtained via the introduced misconfiguration.
A written escalation path, plus confirmation the fix blocks it.
writeupPrompts: Which real-world misconfiguration does the one you introduced most resemble?

missions.title: Crack Your Own Hashes
missions.objective: Measure how fast weak vs. strong passwords actually fall to offline cracking.

target.label: The VM from Snapshot First

missions.resourceNote: Depends on Snapshot First being done first.
steps: Create a handful of test accounts in the VM with a range of passwords: a common weak one, an 8-char 'complex-looking' one, a long random passphrase.
Export the shadow hashes (`sudo cat /etc/shadow`, your own VM only) for those test accounts.
Run `hashcat`/`John` against them with a public wordlist + rule set, and time how long each falls (or doesn't, within a reasonable time budget).
Build a comparison table: password → crack time.
Restore the snapshot afterward.
legalBoundaries: Only crack hashes you generated yourself, in your own VM, for this exercise. Never run a cracker against a real leaked hash dump, even 'just to see' — downloading and cracking breach data you have no authorization over is its own legal problem.

risks.label: GPU-bound cracking can run your machine hot/loud for a while
risks.mitigation: Set a time budget per hash rather than letting it run indefinitely.

completionCriteria: A crack-time comparison table across at least 3 password strengths.
writeupPrompts: What's the actual takeaway for your own real passwords after seeing these numbers?

missions.title: Calculer l'entropie d'un mot de passe — Coder la théorie de la force des mots de passe
missions.objective: Dans le cadre de platinum-crack-your-own-hashes, écrire un script qui calcule l'entropie d'un mot de passe (en Python) et prédit s'il est 'cassable rapidement' selon l'entropie, avant même de lancer hashcat. Comprendre la théorie de la force des mots de passe de façon programmée.

target.label: The VM from Snapshot First

steps: Écris un script Python qui calcule l'entropie d'un mot de passe (en bits) selon la formule : E = L * log2(N) où L est la longueur et N est le nombre de caractères possibles (selon le charset utilisé).
Génère des comptes de test avec des mots de passe de différents niveaux (faible, complexe mais court, long random passphrase).
Calcule l'entropie pour chaque et prédit le temps de cassage (estimé).
Compare avec les résultats réels de hashcat — tes prédictions sont-elles correctes ?
Note: cet exercice t'apprend la cryptographie appliquée et la programmation de sécurité.
legalBoundaries: Only test passwords you create for this exercise.

risks.label: None — local VM only

completionCriteria: A working entropy calculator script.
Comparison between predicted and actual crack times.
writeupPrompts: What's the most important takeaway for your own passwords after seeing these numbers?
How would you extend your entropy calculator to detect common patterns (dictionary words, repeated chars, etc.)?

title: Mobile & Application Security
tagline: Your phone in your pocket, your target on your bench.
summary: Security review of your own phone and the apps installed on it — permissions, decompilation, and traffic inspection.

missions.title: Permission Audit
missions.objective: Review every app on your own phone's permissions and flag over-permissioned ones.

target.label: Your own phone (Android or iOS)

steps: Android: Settings → Privacy → Permission manager, review by permission type (location, mic, contacts, etc.).
iOS: Settings → Privacy & Security, same idea per category.
For each sensitive permission, ask: does this app actually need this to function? Revoke or downgrade to 'while using' anything that doesn't.
Build an audit table: app, permission, justified? action taken.
legalBoundaries: Your own device only.

risks.label: Revoking a permission can break a feature you rely on
risks.mitigation: Test the app after revoking; re-grant if something breaks that you actually need.

completionCriteria: An audit table covering every installed app with a sensitive permission.
writeupPrompts: Which app had the most permissions it clearly didn't need?

missions.title: APK Autopsy
missions.objective: Decompile one of your own installed Android apps and look for hardcoded secrets, insecure storage, or exported components.

target.label: An APK you built, or an app you installed on your own Android device

missions.resourceNote: Android-specific. If you're on iOS-only, the equivalent (class-dump / Frida against an IPA) needs a jailbroken device and is a much higher barrier — treat it as an optional advanced substitute, flagged as a resource gap for now.
steps: Pull the APK (`adb shell pm path <package>` then `adb pull`), or export it from a project you built.
Decompile with `jadx-gui` and read through for hardcoded API keys, secrets, or internal URLs baked into strings.
Check `AndroidManifest.xml` for exported Activities/Services/Receivers that shouldn't be exported, and any `android:debuggable="true"` left on in a release build.
Check where the app stores data (`/data/data/<package>/`, on a rooted device or emulator) for anything sensitive stored unencrypted.
Write up findings and fixes (move secrets server-side, un-export components that don't need it, encrypt local storage).
legalBoundaries: Only decompile apps you built yourself, or that you're licensed/entitled to reverse-engineer for personal security research on your own installed copy — check the app's ToS if it's third-party; when in doubt, do this against your own app.

risks.label: None if scoped to your own app/device

completionCriteria: A findings list from the decompiled APK, plus fix recommendations.
writeupPrompts: Did you find anything in the decompiled code you didn't expect to still be there?

missions.title: Proxy the Phone
missions.objective: Route your own phone's traffic through an intercepting proxy to see what your installed apps actually send.

target.label: Your own phone + PC on the same LAN

tools: manual CA cert install on the phone
steps: Start `mitmproxy` (or Burp's proxy) on your PC, note its LAN IP and port.
On your phone, set the Wi-Fi manual proxy to that IP:port, then install and trust the proxy's CA certificate (needed to see HTTPS traffic in plaintext).
Use a handful of your installed apps normally while capturing.
Look for cleartext credentials, unexpected third-party trackers/SDKs, or tokens sent somewhere surprising.
Remove the proxy config and CA trust when done.
legalBoundaries: Your own device and your own traffic only.

risks.label: Some apps use certificate pinning and will simply stop working while the proxy is active — expected, not a bug
risks.mitigation: Remove proxy settings to restore normal function.

completionCriteria: A traffic report: any cleartext creds found? any unexpected third-party destinations?
writeupPrompts: Which app sent traffic to a destination you didn't expect?

missions.title: Modifier et recompiler un APK — Le cycle complet de modification mobile
missions.objective: Prendre un APK que tu as analysé dans diamond-apk-autopsy, le modifier (changer un texte, désactiver une permission dans le Manifest, modifier une constante), le recompiler avec apktool, le re-signer, et l'installer sur ton téléphone. Apprendre le cycle complet : décompilation → modification → recompilation → signature → installation.

target.label: An APK you built, or an app you installed on your own Android device

steps: Prends un APK que tu as déjà analysé (dans diamond-apk-autopsy).
Décompile-le avec apktool pour obtenir les ressources et le code.
Modifie quelque chose : un texte dans `res/values/strings.xml`, une permission dans `AndroidManifest.xml`, une constante dans le code.
Recompile avec apktool.
Re-signe l'APK avec uber-apk-signer ou apksigner.
Installe l'APK modifié sur ton téléphone avec adb et vérifie que les modifications sont appliquées.
Note: cet exercice t'apprend le cycle complet de modification d'APK, une compétence clé en sécurité mobile.
legalBoundaries: Only modify apps you built yourself, or that you're licensed to reverse-engineer for personal security research on your own installed copy.

risks.label: None if scoped to your own app/device

completionCriteria: A modified APK installed and working on your device.
Documentation of the modifications made and the recompilation process.
writeupPrompts: What was the hardest part of the recompilation process?
How would you detect that an APK has been modified (integrity verification)?

title: Red Team Capstone — Assume Breach, Then Defend
tagline: Chain it, break it, then lock it down like a pro.
summary: The capstone: a multi-service lab, a full chained attack path from foothold to objective, a real pentest report — and then the actual mastery test, flipping to Blue Team and proving every hole is patched.

missions.title: Build the Range
missions.objective: Design and stand up a small multi-service Docker Compose lab (web frontend + internal API + database) with a deliberate, layered vulnerability chain.

target.label: A Docker Compose stack you design yourself

missions.resourceNote: Not bundled in Apihack v1 — this is intentionally left to you to build, reusing the vulnerability patterns from Silver (web) and Platinum (privesc). This mission ships as a brief + grading checklist; the target stack itself is on you.
steps: Design 3 layers: an internet-facing web app with one real bug (from Silver's playbook), an internal-only admin API that's only reachable after the first foothold, and a DB/host layer that needs a privesc-style bug (from Platinum's playbook) to fully compromise.
Build it in Docker Compose so it's disposable and resettable (`docker compose down -v && docker compose up` = clean slate).
Do NOT expose this stack beyond localhost/your own lab network.
legalBoundaries: Entirely your own build, entirely local.

risks.label: None if kept local-only
risks.mitigation: Never publish the compose stack's ports beyond 127.0.0.1.

completionCriteria: A running 3-layer Docker Compose lab with a documented intended attack path.

missions.title: Full Chain
missions.objective: Execute the complete attack path end-to-end, from an assumed low-privilege foothold to the capstone objective, documenting every step.

target.label: The lab from Build the Range

missions.resourceNote: Depends on Build the Range being complete.
tools: Whatever the lab's vulnerabilities call for — Burp/ZAP, linpeas, GTFOBins, etc.
steps: Start from the assumed foothold (e.g. the web app's public bug).
Pivot to the internal API using what the foothold exposes.
Escalate privileges on the host/DB layer using the privesc bug you built in.
Screenshot or log every step as you go — this becomes the evidence trail for the report.
legalBoundaries: Your own lab only.

risks.label: None — disposable local lab

completionCriteria: A complete, evidenced attack chain from foothold to objective.

missions.title: The Report
missions.objective: Write an actual professional-grade penetration test report for the Full Chain engagement.

target.label: Documentation of the Full Chain engagement

missions.resourceNote: Depends on Full Chain being complete.
steps: Write an executive summary (non-technical, for a hypothetical stakeholder): what was tested, what was found, overall risk.
List findings by severity, each with a CVSS-style score, a reproduction PoC, and a concrete remediation.
Add a 'timeline' section mirroring the Full Chain steps.
This is the actual deliverable real pentesters submit to clients — hold it to that bar.
legalBoundaries: n/a — documentation exercise.

risks.label: None

completionCriteria: A complete written report: exec summary, findings by severity, PoCs, remediations, timeline.

missions.title: Blue Team Flip
missions.objective: Patch every vulnerability you exploited in the lab, then re-run Full Chain and prove it now fails at every step.

target.label: The lab from Build the Range, now being hardened

missions.resourceNote: Depends on The Report being complete.
tools: Same stack as Build the Range
steps: Go through your own report's remediation list and apply every fix to the lab.
Re-run the exact Full Chain steps against the patched lab.
Confirm each step now fails, and document why (what specifically blocks it now).
This is the actual completion criterion for Master rank: you're not done until you can no longer break your own system.
legalBoundaries: Your own lab only.

risks.label: None

completionCriteria: Every step of Full Chain confirmed blocked against the patched lab, with a short 'why this now fails' note per step.
writeupPrompts: Looking back across all six ranks, which single fix habit will you carry into every future project by default?

missions.title: Orchestrer la chaîne d'attaque avec un script — Coder un outil de pentest minimal
missions.objective: Une fois le lab Master construit, écrire un script (Python avec requests, ou Node.js) qui orchestre les étapes de l'attaque de manière partiellement automatisée : exécuter la première vulnérabilité, parser le résultat, utiliser ce résultat pour la prochaine étape, etc. Ce script devient ton propre outil de pentest minimal.

target.label: The lab from Build the Range

steps: Écris un script qui commence par exploiter la première vulnérabilité du lab (ex: SQLi sur le web app).
Parse le résultat pour extraire les informations nécessaires à la prochaine étape (ex: credentials, tokens, IDs).
Utilise ces informations pour attaquer la prochaine couche (ex: API interne).
Continue jusqu'à l'objectif final, en documentant chaque étape dans le script.
Ajoute des logs et des outputs formatés pour que le script soit lisible et réutilisable.
Optionnel: ajoute une fonction de 'dry run' qui simule l'attaque sans l'exécuter réellement.
legalBoundaries: Only run against your own lab.

risks.label: None — local lab only

completionCriteria: A working exploit chain script that automates the attack path.
Documentation of the script architecture and how to extend it.
writeupPrompts: What did you learn about attack orchestration by writing this script?
How would you extend this script to support multiple targets or multiple attack paths?
